title: Attention Sinks as Internal Signals for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models
claim: Per-head attention-sink scores are sorted, top-k selected, and concatenated into one feature vector that a probe classifies as hallucinated or not.
layout: Single row, left-to-right, parallel per-head branches merging into concat, then probe
description: A left-to-right pipeline diagram. At the far left, a rounded gray box titled 'Sink scores' holds a lower-triangular attention matrix. Its cells are shaded in blues and outlined in red, and a red downward arrow sits beside it. Next to the matrix is the formula sum_{u=i}^T a_ui / (T-i). Arrows fan out to three parallel rows, s^(0,0), s^(0,1) and s^(L,H), separated by an ellipsis. Each row shows a strip of four cells colored from pale yellow to orange or red. Each strip feeds sequentially into 'sort' and 'top-k' boxes. The three branches converge on a gray 'Concat' box, which outputs a green strip labeled z. A downward arrow leads to a blue 'Hallucination Probe' box. A final arrow points left to a yellow label reading 'hallucination / no hallucination', in red and green text.
caption: Pipeline for hallucination detection based on attention sink scores. For each layer $l$ and head $h$, we compute sink scores $s^{(l,h)}$, defined as the average of attention scores directed toward each token position. These scores are then sorted, and the top-$k$ values are selected as features. The selected features from all layers and heads are concatenated to form the final feature vector $z$, which is passed to a hallucination probe -- a binary classifier trained on labeled examples to distinguish hallucinated outputs from factually correct ones at inference time.
abstract: Large language models frequently exhibit hallucinations: fluent and confident outputs that are factually incorrect or unsupported by the input context. While recent hallucination detection methods have explored various features derived from attention maps, the underlying mechanisms they exploit remain poorly understood. In this work, we propose SinkProbe, a hallucination detection method grounded in the observation that hallucinations are deeply entangled with attention sinks - tokens that accumulate disproportionate attention mass during generation - indicating a transition from distributed, input-grounded attention to compressed, prior-dominated computation. Importantly, although sink scores are computed solely from attention maps, we find that the classifier preferentially relies on sinks whose associated value vectors have large norms. Moreover, we show that previous methods implicitly depend on attention sinks by establishing their mathematical relationship to sink scores. Our findings yield a novel hallucination detection method grounded in theory that produces state-of-the-art results across popular datasets and LLMs.
